lesson.body:
Almost every pairing guideline you have ever heard is a rough proxy for one idea: neither the food nor the wine should flatten the other.

Delicate food wants a light wine. Steamed fish, salads and fresh cheeses go with crisp, light-bodied whites, because a big oaky red would simply erase them. Rich food wants a fuller wine — a slow-cooked stew or a well-marbled steak can stand up to something dense and structured.

This is what the old "red with meat, white with fish" line is clumsily pointing at. It is right often enough to survive, and wrong often enough to be worth ignoring: a rich salmon dish is happier with a light red than with a delicate white, and roast chicken sits comfortably with either.

Weight is also easier to judge than flavour. You do not need to identify notes in the glass. You only need to ask whether it feels light or heavy.

Match light food to light wine, rich to fuller
Judge a wine's weight without naming its flavours

deep_notes: Wine professionals call a wine's weight its body, and describe it as light, medium or full. Alcohol is the biggest driver: a wine at 14.5% usually feels noticeably fuller than one at 11%. Sugar, oak and tannin (the drying grip from grape skins) can add to the feeling of weight too. A handy comparison is milk: skimmed, semi-skimmed and whole milk feel roughly like light, medium and full body.

How a dish is cooked changes its weight as much as what it is. Steaming and poaching keep food light, while roasting, grilling and slow braising make it richer. The same piece of fish feels lighter poached than fried in butter. With steak there is a second effect: the protein and fat in the meat soften tannin, the drying grip in red wine, which is why a firm red sits so comfortably beside it.

The classic proof is salmon with Pinot Noir, a grape that makes light-bodied reds with little tannin, the drying grip found in many reds. Low tannin matters, because a tannic red with oily fish can taste metallic. The rule fails the other way too: pork and veal are meats, yet they often suit a rich white such as an oaked Chardonnay. Roast chicken happily takes a white or a light red, which shows the rule's blind spot in a single dish.

The label gives you a head start before you even sip. Alcohol is a good clue: a wine under about 12% usually feels light, while one over about 14% usually feels full. Where the grapes grew helps too. Warm, sunny regions ripen grapes more, so their wines tend to be fuller, while cool regions tend to give lighter wines. Then sip and notice whether the wine feels thin and watery or round and mouth-filling.

deeper.body: Pros keep two ideas apart. Body is how heavy a wine feels in the mouth. Flavour intensity is how strong its taste and smell are. They often travel together, but not always. A Mosel Riesling can be very light in body yet bursting with flavour. So a pro matches both: how heavy the dish is, and how loud its flavours are.
deeper.title: Weight is not flavour

deeper.q: A wine that is light in body must also be mild in flavour.
deeper.why: Body and flavour intensity are separate things. A Mosel Riesling can be light in body and still bursting with flavour.

deeper.body: Ageing a white wine in oak barrels, or leaving it on its lees (the spent yeast left after fermentation), makes it rounder and creamier. That is why a rich, oaked Chardonnay feels far fuller than a crisp Chablis, which is often unoaked, even though Chablis is made from Chardonnay too. Same grape, different weight, different dish.
deeper.title: Winemakers can build weight

v2.body:
From 1987 to 2024, winemakers and wine lovers gathered most summers in McMinnville, Oregon, for the **International Pinot Noir Celebration**. One of its best-loved traditions was a salmon bake: wild salmon roasted on wooden alder stakes over a big open fire. The wine poured with the fish was Pinot Noir, a red. The old saying "white with fish" would call that a mistake. It works beautifully, and the reason is the one rule in this lesson.

Almost every pairing guideline you have ever heard is a rough stand-in for one idea: neither the food nor the wine should flatten the other. So you match their **weight**, meaning how light or heavy each one feels in your mouth. For wine, weight is what tasters call **body**: light, medium or full. The rule works both ways. A big wine can erase a delicate dish, and a rich dish can make a light wine taste thin and watery.

Delicate food wants a light wine. Steamed fish, salads and fresh cheeses go with crisp, light-bodied whites, because a big oaky red would simply erase them. Rich food wants a fuller wine: a slow-cooked stew or a **well-marbled** steak (one with streaks of fat running through the meat) can stand up to something dense and full. Roast chicken sits in the middle.

How a dish is cooked changes its weight as much as what it is. Steaming and poaching keep food light, while roasting, grilling, frying and slow braising make it richer. The same fish feels lighter poached than fried in butter.

This is what the old "red with meat, white with fish" line is clumsily pointing at. It is right often enough to survive, and wrong often enough to be worth ignoring. A rich salmon dish is happier with a light red, such as Pinot Noir, than with a delicate white. Roast chicken sits comfortably with either. Pork and veal are meats, yet they often suit a rich white such as an **oaked Chardonnay** (a white wine aged in oak barrels, which makes it rounder and fuller). Ask how rich the dish is, not which animal is on the plate.

Weight is also easier to judge than flavour. You do not need to name **flavour notes**, the separate flavours in a wine. Take a sip and ask: does this feel light or heavy? Then ask the same of the food, and match the answers. The label gives you a head start: a wine under about 12% alcohol usually feels light, and one over about 14% usually feels full. Wines from warm, sunny places tend to be fuller than wines from cool ones.
deep_notes: The International Pinot Noir Celebration began in 1987, when a group of Oregon winemakers looked for a way to show off their wine. For decades it was held each summer on the Linfield campus in McMinnville, with winemakers from Burgundy and many other places pouring beside the Oregon producers. The 2024 edition was its last in that form. At the salmon bake, wild salmon was cooked on wooden stakes over a wood fire, a traditional Pacific Northwest method.

Wine professionals call a wine's weight its body, and describe it as light, medium or full. Alcohol is the biggest driver: a wine at 14.5% usually feels noticeably fuller than one at 11%. Sugar, oak and tannin (the drying feel from grape skins) can add to the feeling of weight too. Food has the same range: a clear broth, a creamy soup and a thick stew are all soups, yet each feels heavier than the last.

Here is a quick test at the table. Take a bite, then a sip. If the dish seems to go quiet and all you notice is the wine, the wine is too heavy. If the wine suddenly tastes thin, sharp or watery, the food is too heavy for it. When both still taste like themselves, the weights match. You are not hunting for a perfect match, only avoiding a lopsided one.

Fat and richness are what give a dish its weight. That is why oily fish such as salmon or mackerel feel heavier than white fish such as cod or sole, and why a well-marbled steak feels richer than a lean one. Butter, cream and cheese push a dish up the scale. Fresh, raw and green things, like salads, pull it down. Most everyday dishes sit in the middle, where a medium-bodied wine is a safe choice.

Steaming and poaching add no fat and no browning, so the food stays as light as it began. Roasting, grilling and frying add browned, savoury flavours and often fat, and slow braising concentrates a dish into something rich and deep. With steak there is a second effect: the fat and protein in the meat soften the drying feel of a red's tannin, which is why a firm red sits so comfortably beside it.

The classic proof is salmon with Pinot Noir, a grape that makes light-bodied reds with little tannin. Low tannin matters, because a tannic red with oily fish can taste metallic. The rule fails the other way too: pork and veal are meats, yet they often suit a rich white such as an oaked Chardonnay. Roast chicken happily takes a white or a light red, which shows the rule's blind spot in a single dish.

Alcohol is the best single clue because it makes wine slightly thicker and warmer in the mouth. Climate works through ripeness: sun builds sugar in the grapes, and yeast turns more sugar into more alcohol. So a Chardonnay from cool Chablis usually feels leaner than one from a warm, sunny place. After the label, sip and notice whether the wine feels thin and watery or round and mouth-filling.

A Mosel Riesling can be very light in body yet bursting with flavour. So a pro matches both: how heavy the dish is, and how loud its flavours are.

steps.q: Two bottles for a rich beef stew: one at 11.5% alcohol, one at 14.5%. Which is the likelier match, and why?
steps.why: Alcohol is the label's best clue to weight, so the stronger bottle can stand up to a rich stew.

cards.back: How light or heavy a food or a wine feels in your mouth.
